# 01 Overview {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## CP Pilot Course

- CP4285 is part of the **CP428x Emerging Topics in Computer Science** series at NUS Computing
- These are **pilot courses**, each run for a single semester, with the intention of eventually becoming a permanent offering
- Students should expect the course is **not yet fully mature** — content, assessments, and delivery are actively evolving
- The series exists to expose undergraduates to **emerging areas** before they become established curriculum

## Ethics Thread

- Ethical issues are **not an afterthought** — they are woven throughout every week
- Core themes we will revisit: **bias, fairness, privacy, exposure, transparency, stakeholder impact**
- Recommendation systems shape everyday decisions: what people read, watch, buy, apply for, and who receives attention and opportunities

::: {.callout-warning}
These systems encode values and trade-offs. Understanding how they work means understanding what they optimise for — and at whose expense.
:::

# 04 Types of Recommendation Systems {background-color="#EF7C00"}

## A Card-Suit Framework for User Types

We can think about different **user archetypes** using a card-suit analogy:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
♠ **Spades — The Explorer**
- Seeks novelty and diversity
- Values serendipitous discovery
- Dislikes filter bubbles

♥ **Hearts — The Social Connector**
- Influenced by friends and community
- Trusts collaborative signals
- Values shared tastes
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
♦ **Diamonds — The Pragmatist**
- Goal-oriented, task-driven
- Wants the most relevant result fast
- Values precision over diversity

♣ **Clubs — The Loyalist**
- Sticks to known preferences
- Values consistency and familiarity
- Resistant to change
:::
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): How did Min introduce this framework? Was it from a specific paper or his own framing? Were there other user types discussed? -->
:::

## Matching Systems to User Types

Different recommendation paradigms serve different user archetypes:

| User Type | Best-Suited Approach | Key Objective |
|-----------|---------------------|---------------|
| ♠ Explorer | Diversity-aware / serendipity models | Novelty, coverage |
| ♥ Social Connector | Collaborative filtering, social graphs | Community similarity |
| ♦ Pragmatist | Retrieval-ranking pipelines | Precision, relevance |
| ♣ Loyalist | Content-based filtering | Consistency, familiarity |

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): Did Min discuss how real systems handle mixed user types, or how user types can shift over time? -->
:::

## Classical Recommendation Paradigms

::: {.incremental}
- **Popularity-based:** Recommend globally popular items — no personalisation
- **Content-based filtering:** Recommend items similar to what the user has liked, based on item features
- **Collaborative filtering (CF):** Leverage patterns across many users — no item features needed
- **Hybrid approaches:** Combine multiple signals for robustness
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): What specific examples or datasets did Min use to illustrate each paradigm? Were there any live demos? -->
:::

## The Cold-Start Problem

::: {.incremental}
- **New user cold-start:** No interaction history → cannot personalise
- **New item cold-start:** No ratings → cannot appear in CF recommendations
- **System cold-start:** Entirely new platform with no data
:::

**Strategies:**
- Use content features (bypasses interaction requirement)
- Ask users for explicit preferences onboarding
- Fall back to popularity-based recommendations

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): Were any specific industry solutions to cold-start discussed (e.g., onboarding surveys, zero-shot approaches)? -->
:::

## Ethics Thread: Popularity Bias and Exposure Inequality

- Popular items get recommended → more interactions → even more popular (**feedback loop**)
- Long-tail items receive little to no exposure
- Who bears the cost? **Niche creators, minority preferences, new entrants**

::: {.callout-warning}
Recommendation objectives that optimise purely for engagement can systematically disadvantage underrepresented content.
:::

## Summary

| Method | Personalised? | Needs Item Features? | Cold-Start Robust? |
|--------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Popularity | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ |
| Content-Based | ✓ | ✓ | Partial |
| User-Based CF | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Item-Based CF | ✓ | ✗ | Partial |
